text: An equinox is one of the two days each year when daytime and night-time are almost exactly the same length everywhere on Earth. The name comes from Latin words meaning equal night. One falls around September 23rd, the other around March 20th; after the September one, nights in the northern half of the world are longer than days.

Glum means quietly gloomy or low, with the spark gone out of you. A glum person is not shouting or crying, just flat and disappointed. Calling the equinox a glum milestone is the writer's way of saying it marks the start of the dark, cold half of the year.

A milestone was once a real stone by the roadside telling travellers how far they had come. Now it means any point that marks how far along something is, like a birthday, a hundredth goal, or the first day of a season.

A hemisphere is half a ball, and for Earth it means half the planet: the northern hemisphere is everything above the equator, the southern hemisphere everything below. The two halves have opposite seasons, so September brings autumn to the north and spring to the south.

When something begins in earnest, it starts properly and seriously after a slow or half-hearted start. Practice might start in earnest once the season's first game is scheduled. Here the winter gloom begins in earnest after the equinox, meaning the real darkness starts now.

Gloom is dimness, a lack of light, and it also means a heavy, sad mood. English often uses the one word for both, which is why the darkness of winter and feeling low about it sound the same. In this article, winter gloom means the dark months themselves.

To supplement something is to add extra to it, and a supplement is that extra bit. In health, supplements are vitamins and minerals sold in pills or drops, taken on top of ordinary food. The whole article is about whether those extras actually help.

Ultraviolet, or UV, is a kind of light that human eyes cannot see, just past the violet end of the rainbow. It carries more energy than visible light, which is why it can burn skin and also why it can start the chemical reactions that build vitamin D.

In chemistry a compound is a substance built from two or more kinds of atom joined together, like water or sugar. Calling vitamin D a compound simply means it is one particular chemical. Watch out for the other meanings of compound, which include a walled group of buildings and to make something worse.
Vital means necessary for life, not just useful. It comes from vita, the Latin word for life, the same root as vitamin. A compound vital for health is one the body genuinely cannot do without.

Something on the market is available for people to buy. A house on the market is up for sale; a new phone on the market is in the shops. Saying vitamin D is one of the most popular supplements on the market means it is among the best-selling of everything on offer.

Among scientists a paper is not a sheet of paper but a written report of a piece of research, published so other scientists can read and check it. Researchers spend months on one paper. A paper published in 2017 means a study whose results came out that year.

A dose is the measured amount of a medicine or vitamin taken at one time. Doses matter enormously: the same substance can do nothing in a small dose and harm you in a huge one. Large doses here means far more than the body actually needs.

Writers use the stuff as a casual way of saying that substance again without repeating its name. Levels of the stuff means levels of vitamin D. It is informal, the kind of phrase you would use talking to a friend.

A stamp of approval is official permission or backing, from the days when an approved document got a real stamp pressed onto it. When a government gives supplements its stamp of approval, it is publicly saying they are a good idea.

In everyday speech a theory is a guess, but in science it means a worked-out explanation of how something happens, built on evidence. Good medical theory behind vitamin D means scientists had solid reasons to expect it to work. The article's point is that even good theory has to be tested on real people.

In theory means the way something should work going by the reasoning; in practice means what actually happens when you try it. The pair is used to point out a gap between the two. Vitamin D looked excellent in theory and did nothing in practice.

Rickets is a disease of childhood in which bones stay soft instead of hardening, so growing legs bend outward under the body's weight. It is caused by a lack of vitamin D, because without it the body cannot take in enough calcium from food. It was common in smoky, sunless industrial cities and is rare today.
To deform is to lose the proper shape and be bent or twisted out of it. A plastic ruler left on a hot radiator will deform. Bones that soften and deform have bent out of their normal straight shape.

A receptor is a molecule on or inside a cell that a particular substance fits into, like a key fitting a lock. When the substance lands in the receptor, it sets off a change inside that cell. Finding vitamin-D receptors all over the body suggested vitamin D was doing jobs in many organs.

The intestines are the long coiled tubes below your stomach where food is broken down further and the useful parts pass through the wall into your blood. Together they run about seven metres in an adult. Vitamin D does much of its work there, helping calcium make that crossing.

Something influential has the power to change what other people think or do. It does not mean correct. The influential studies here set the direction of research for thirty years, and were still wrong.

Significantly means by a large enough amount to matter and not just by chance. Scientists use it strictly: a significant difference is one big enough that plain luck is an unlikely explanation. Deaths significantly more common in northern states means the gap was too big to shrug off.

To inhibit something is to slow it down or hold it back rather than stop it dead. Cold weather inhibits the growth of most plants. Animal studies suggested vitamin D could inhibit the growth of cancer cells, meaning make them multiply more slowly.

A trial in medicine is a carefully run test of a treatment on real people, usually with one group getting the treatment and another getting nothing, so the two can be compared. Trials take years and cost a fortune, and they are the only way to find out whether something actually works. Three of them failed vitamin D.

These are the names of the three biggest vitamin-D trials ever run, in America, Australia and New Zealand. Between them they followed tens of thousands of people for several years each. Big studies with catchy short names are normal in medicine.

This is one of the most respected medical magazines in the world, where doctors publish and read about new research. Something appearing there carries weight with the whole profession. Despite the New England name, it is read everywhere.

An editorial is a piece in which the publication itself sums up a situation and says what it thinks, rather than simply reporting the news. In a medical journal, an editorial often gathers up several studies and says what they add up to. That is what this 2022 one did for vitamin D.

Here falls does not mean autumn or dropping: it means older people falling over, which is a serious cause of broken bones. Doctors test whether a treatment can prevent falls because a bad fall can change an older person's life. Vitamin D did not.

To stave something off is to keep it away or hold it back for a while, from an old word for fighting something off with a stick. You might eat a snack to stave off hunger until dinner. Vitamin D did not stave off the sniffles.

The sniffles is a light-hearted name for a mild cold, the runny-nose, sniffing kind rather than anything serious. Using it here keeps the sentence casual while listing what vitamin D failed to prevent.

Deficient means short of something you need. A diet deficient in iron does not have enough of it. People mildly deficient in vitamin D have less than doctors would like, though not so little that they are ill.
Beneficial means doing good, being helpful. It comes from the same root as benefit. No beneficial effects means the supplements did nothing good that researchers could measure.

A fracture is a break or crack in a bone. Doctors use the word for everything from a hairline crack to a bone snapped in two. Since weak bones fracture more easily, researchers expected vitamin D to bring fractures down, and it did not.

Medics is a British word for doctors and other medical professionals. American English usually saves medic for someone giving emergency treatment, in the army or an ambulance. The Economist is British, so here it just means doctors.
Sufficiently means enough, to the degree needed. The body is sufficiently complicated that doctors can only guess means it is complicated enough that guessing is all they can manage.

An educated guess is a guess made by someone who knows the subject, so it is far better than a random one but still not knowledge. A doctor predicting how a new drug will behave is making an educated guess. The article's point is that even expert guesses need testing.

Saying there is no substitute for something means nothing else will do the job in its place. There is no substitute for practice. Here, nothing replaces actually giving a drug to lots of people and watching what happens.

The equator is the imaginary line around the middle of the Earth, halfway between the North and South Poles. Sunlight arrives most directly there, so countries near it get strong sun all year. The further you live from it, the weaker your winter sunlight.
Diet here does not mean trying to lose weight. It means simply the food a person normally eats. Getting vitamin D from your diet means getting it from ordinary meals, such as fish, eggs and red meat.

To surge is to rise suddenly and strongly, the way a wave swells and rushes forward. It is used for crowds, prices, electricity and illnesses alike. Colds surge in winter means the number of people catching one shoots up in the cold months.
